title: Haematinics
subtitle: Ferritin, transferrin saturation, B12 and folate
summary: Ferritin, transferrin saturation, B12 and folate
introduction: Interpret ferritin, transferrin saturation, B12 and folate with FBC indices, CRP/inflammation, renal/liver disease, diet, bleeding history and neurological symptoms.

rows.name: Ferritin
rows.referenceRange: Low ferritin strongly supports iron deficiency; exact cut-off laboratory/context dependent
notes: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein and may be normal or raised despite iron deficiency during infection, inflammation, liver disease or malignancy.

rows.name: Transferrin saturation
notes: Low saturation with low ferritin supports absolute iron deficiency. Low saturation with normal/high ferritin may reflect inflammation, CKD or mixed deficiency.

rows.name: Vitamin B12
notes: Deficiency can produce macrocytosis, glossitis, paraesthesia, impaired vibration/proprioception, gait disturbance, cognitive change or pancytopenia. Neurological deficiency can occur without anaemia or macrocytosis.

rows.name: Folate
notes: Low folate can cause macrocytic anaemia. Replace B12 deficiency first or concurrently; folate alone can improve anaemia while neurological B12 injury progresses.

urgentFindings: Anaemia with chest pain, syncope, breathlessness at rest, hypotension or active bleeding.
New gait disturbance, objective sensory loss, weakness, cognitive change or bladder/bowel symptoms with possible B12 deficiency.
Pancytopenia, rapidly falling haemoglobin or platelets, or haemolysis features (jaundice, dark urine, raised bilirubin/LDH).
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.
